clue.text: Can't hope for a shake up in Whitehall?

definitions.note: the definition names the monument by where it stands, so it reads as 'the thing in Whitehall'

indicators.note: to shake up is to jumble things, so the letters of the two words before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cynic wonders whether there is no hope of a government reshuffle in Whitehall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shake up' tells you to rearrange the letters of CAN'T HOPE. 'Whitehall' looks like shorthand for the civil service, but here it is the London street itself, and the definition is the monument standing in it.
explanation.definitionFit: The national war memorial stands in the middle of Whitehall, the London street lined with government offices.

clue.text: Neil Kinnock about to ditch family with no money

indicators.note: about here means moved around, so the letters left over are rearranged
to ditch is to get rid of, so the family word and the word no are taken out of the name

parts.note: your kin are your family
taken as written: the clue's own word no is removed too

explanation.surface: Neil Kinnock, the Labour leader, is about to abandon his family and is left penniless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To ditch' takes KIN and NO out of NEIL KINNOCK, leaving NEILCK, and 'about' rearranges those six letters. 'With no money' looks like being broke, but 'no' is removed and 'money' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A nickel is the American five-cent coin, so it is a piece of money.

clue.text: New York for the greedy consumer?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the city's well-known nickname
second meaning, playful: a large piece of fruit is what a greedy eater would want

explanation.walkthrough: The second half reads the city's nickname literally, as an outsized fruit for a glutton.
explanation.definitionFit: The Big Apple is the familiar nickname for New York City, and taken literally it is a large fruit.

clue.text: The Family cast a warm glow in Berkshire

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the House of ..., the British royal family

definitions.text: cast a warm glow in Berkshire
definitions.meaning: second meaning: ... Castle, in the county of Berkshire, which burned in a famous fire in 1992

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast a warm glow' is a sly nod to the 1992 fire at Windsor Castle; Berkshire is the English county west of London where the castle stands.
explanation.definitionFit: Windsor is the surname of the British royal family and also the Berkshire town whose castle caught fire.

clue.text: Without Walls will show Pope fooling around with a novice nun heartlessly

indicators.note: fooling around suggests messing about, so the gathered letters are jumbled

parts.note: L is a learner, the letter on a learner driver's plate

indicators.note: heartlessly means the middle letter is cut out, leaving the first and last of the word nun

parts.note: the word nun, whose middle letter is about to be dropped

explanation.surface: A TV arts programme shows the Pope messing about with a young nun.
explanation.walkthrough: Without Walls was a Channel 4 arts series, so the capitals disguise a plain description of a room. 'Heartlessly' sounds like cruelty to the nun, but it only removes her middle letter, leaving NN for 'fooling around' to mix in.
explanation.definitionFit: An open-plan office or home has no internal partition walls between its spaces.

clue.text: Minister — combination of Conservative, Liberal and Heffer

parts.note: Eric Heffer was a left-wing Labour MP

explanation.surface: A new government minister is a blend of Conservative, Liberal and Labour's Eric Heffer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minister' looks political, but it is the church sense, a member of the clergy.
explanation.definitionFit: A minister of religion is a clergyman, so the word for a churchman fits.

clue.text: Habitual criminal about to join cops on informal "visit"

parts.note: re means about or concerning
CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, the British plain-clothes police

indicators.note: informal suggests loose and casual, so the letters of visit are shuffled

explanation.surface: A repeat offender pays an unofficial call on the police.
explanation.definitionFit: A recidivist is someone who keeps reoffending, so a confirmed lawbreaker who returns to crime.

clue.text: Smart git Liberal that is ruffled by separatists

indicators.note: ruffled means disturbed, so the gathered letters are mixed up

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: A clever Liberal is rattled by a group of breakaway militants.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tamil Tigers fought for an independent Tamil state in northern Sri Lanka, a breakaway movement.

clue.text: See 12
Unfinished sex on beach (tricky positions) into which we delve each issue

definitions.text: into which we delve each issue

indicators.note: unfinished means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: nooky is slang for sex
a beach is made of sand
being in a corner is a tight spot, so corners are awkward positions

explanation.surface: Half-finished beach sex in awkward positions sounds like a tabloid story the magazine digs into each week.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unfinished' drops the last letter of NOOKY to give NOOK. Nooks and Corners is Private Eye's long-running column on architecture and planning, so 'we' is the magazine itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Nooks and corners are out-of-the-way places one searches, and the phrase is also the title of a Private Eye column.

clue.text: Midge clinging to bloke like shit

indicators.note: clinging to means Ure is attached right after the bloke word

parts.note: a bloke is a man
Midge Ure is the Scottish singer of Ultravox who co-organised Live Aid

explanation.surface: A small biting insect sticks to a man like dirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Midge' looks like the insect, but it is the musician Midge Ure, whose surname is 'clinging to' the end of MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Manure is animal dung spread on fields, so it is a polite word for excrement.

clue.text: Supposed indicator of our intentions to have a quick ride (almost) with Ms Toynbee (almost)

indicators.note: almost here means nearly the same word: the spelling differs but it is said exactly alike

parts.note: a gallop is a fast ride on a horse

indicators.note: almost means the name stops one letter short

parts.note: Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

explanation.surface: Pollsters plan a rushed outing with journalist Polly Toynbee, though neither quite happens.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'almost' marks GALLUP, the polling firm, as said just like GALLOP though spelt differently; the second cuts POLLY to POLL. 'Supposed' is a dig: a survey of voting intentions only claims to show what people will do.
explanation.definitionFit: A Gallup poll is an opinion survey that claims to show how people intend to vote.

clue.text: Picture student lying in vomit — an environmental hazard!

parts.note: an oil is an oil painting, a picture

indicators.note: lying in means the student letter sits inside the vomit word

parts.note: sick is vomit
L is a learner, from the learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: An art student is found lying in a pool of sick, a real health risk.
explanation.definitionFit: A slick of spilled crude oil on the sea kills wildlife and pollutes coasts.

clue.text: See 20
Ruthlessly push through merger of public and private transport

parts.note: rail stands for public transport, the trains
road stands for private transport, the car

explanation.surface: A merger of state and private transport firms is forced through.
explanation.definitionFit: To railroad a measure is to force it through quickly without proper debate.

clue.text: See 10
It's pass to hot tongue your ex

parts.note: read as passé, out of date, hence old
a flame is a tongue of fire

explanation.surface: Snogging a former partner is out of fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass' stands for passé, out of fashion. 'Hot tongue' looks like a French kiss but is a tongue of fire.
explanation.definitionFit: An old flame is a former lover, someone you used to go out with.

clue.text: Small bloomers worn by vote-seekers

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a rosette is literally a little rose, a small flower
second meaning: British election candidates wear party-coloured ribbon badges

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomers' looks like underwear, but it means flowers. British candidates wear a coloured ribbon rosette on election day.
explanation.definitionFit: The ribbon badge is named after a little rose, so it covers both the flower and the campaign badge.

clue.text: Leader of small band has turned blue

indicators.note: turned means the three letters of has are rearranged

parts.note: to feel blue is to feel down

explanation.surface: The head of a little group of musicians has become depressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned' rearranges HAS into ASH. The 'small band' is not musicians but the Liberal Democrats, a small party in the Commons led by Paddy Ashdown.
explanation.definitionFit: Paddy Ashdown led the Liberal Democrats, then a small group of MPs.

clue.text: Government's pledge to its suffering people

definitions.text: Government's pledge to its suffering people

parts.words: Government's pledge to its suffering people
parts.note: the sufferers are the sick in hospital, and the pledge is the 1991 NHS document setting out their rights

explanation.walkthrough: 'Suffering people' reads as a cynical dig at citizens in general, but it means those who are ill.
explanation.definitionFit: The Patient's Charter was the Major government's 1991 list of promised standards for NHS patients.

clue.text: Relative disaster with Birt in charge?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an aunt, a family relation
second meaning: the BBC's nickname, which John Birt ran as Director-General

explanation.walkthrough: Auntie is the British nickname for the BBC, run in the 1990s by John Birt; the clue jeers at his management.
explanation.definitionFit: Auntie is a familiar word for a parent's sister and the long-standing nickname of the BBC.

clue.text: Brenda upside down gobbling King starkers

indicators.note: gobbling means swallowing, so the king letter goes inside
in a down clue, upside down means the surname is read from bottom to top

parts.note: Brenda Dean was the leader of the print union SOGAT
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: Brenda, turned head over heels and eating a king, is stark naked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upside down' turns DEAN into NAED, and 'gobbling' puts K inside it. 'Brenda' is Private Eye's name for the Queen, but here it is the union leader Brenda Dean. Starkers is British slang for naked.
explanation.definitionFit: Starkers is jokey British slang for wearing no clothes at all.

clue.text: Can't stand the game of cricket, as they say in Kingston?

indicators.note: Kingston is the capital of Jamaica, where the is said de, so the words are heard in that accent

parts.note: the Test is a Test match, the top level of the game

explanation.surface: A Jamaican cricket fan can't stand the game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As they say in Kingston' asks for a Jamaican accent, where 'the Test' comes out as 'de Test'. A Test match is an international cricket game.
explanation.definitionFit: To detest something is to hate it, to be unable to bear it.

clue.text: See 8
One interpretation of Koran favoured by train-spotters?

definitions.note: a noun phrase in effect: the garment such enthusiasts like

parts.note: one is a, as in a single thing

indicators.note: an interpretation is a new reading, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A particular reading of the Koran is popular with train-spotters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Interpretation of' rearranges A and KORAN. Train-spotters, British railway enthusiasts who log engine numbers, are stereotyped as wearing hooded waterproof jackets.
explanation.definitionFit: The hooded waterproof jacket is the stereotypical garment of a railway enthusiast.

clue.text: 1 Representative in what sounds like food shop scandal

indicators.note: what sounds like means the words are spoken and heard as the answer

parts.note: a deli is a food shop, and a scandal is often named with -gate after Watergate

explanation.surface: A representative is caught up in a scandal at a delicatessen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What sounds like' says to hear the phrase: scandals are named with '-gate' after Watergate, so a scandal at a deli is a 'deli-gate'.
explanation.definitionFit: A delegate is a person sent to act or vote on behalf of others.

clue.text: Elvis alive! (Just one bit of plastic inside)

indicators.note: inside means the letters are found within the phrase Elvis alive

parts.note: the letters run across the two words, from the end of Elvis into the start of alive

explanation.surface: A tabloid headline proclaims Elvis alive, with only a small bit of plastic inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside' points back to the headline 'Elvis alive', which holds the answer within its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Visa is a brand of credit card, one of the plastic cards in a wallet.

clue.text: Toss off Thatcher? Alien, cheap and shoddy!

parts.note: to toss off a drink is to down it
Mark Thatcher is Margaret Thatcher's son
ET is the alien in the Spielberg film

explanation.surface: A rude jeer at Thatcher calls her foreign, cheap and shoddy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thatcher' looks like Margaret, but it is her son Mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Downmarket goods are cheap, low in quality and aimed at the bottom of the market.
